In many ways 2015 was the year of Mad Max. We got the excellent film Mad Max Fury Road earlier in the year closer to May, and in September we recieved Mad Max 2015 by Avalanche studios. The devs behind the Just Cause series. 

When I first heard about this game I hated the idea of it. I didn't really think in the era of Fallout that we really needed another derivative post apocalyptic open world game. When I heard Mel Gibson wasn't involved at all that really made me less interested in it. Then after Fury Road I relaxed to the idea of more Mad Max. And I was surprised by how much I liked this game and what it set out to accomplish. 

In many ways the Mad Max Film series is almost the perfect concept for an open world driving game. You have a post apocalyptic sandbox filled with hostile enemy raiders. You have a core driving experience with car combat and upgrade trees to customize your hot rod. What I was surprised by the most with this game in particular was how much detail was paid attention to. There are numerous little callbacks to the previous films, and the stylistic decisions they made with the game were spot on.

The wasteland of Mad Max was perfectly nailed. Unlike the Fallout games, the world feels very handcrafted. Nothing feels copy-pasted and throwaway locations like enemy outposts all look scenic enough to take a dozen screenshots of. The game also boasts an impressive draw distance and it runs extremely well on PC. The gameplay is solid enough. With car combat being a highlight in the game. There's a very noticeable focus on scavanging. Your car requires gasoline to keep going, you require water inorder to heal yourself. You only ever find individual shells for your gun and can only carry a handful at one time. I really do feel more like a vulture picking at a corpse of a dead world than a super soldier like in most modern sandbox games. 

But with all that said, the game isn't for everyone. I feel alone when I say this but the things people dislike about this game, like the heavy focus on sidequests, the general minimalistic storyline and lack of gunplay are things that appealed to me about it. I actually think the laundry list Assassin's Creed formula benefits this game greatly. Your grand objective in this game isn't a pointless revenge story or a pointless revolutionary story. You spend the vast majority of this game looking for ways to upgrade your car. I like how the game focuses on that rather than a more generic storyline and mission structure.

As I said the game isn't for everyone. If you're not a fan of the Mad Max films and you get turned off by a heavy focus on sidequests with a game I'd suggest looking elsewhere. I'd wager less than 10% of Mad Max is actual story content and if that sounds like a bad thing, you will probably find a lot of this game very tedious.

Although there was a bit of hassle with the midnight release. The game is finally out! I haven't spent to much time with the game, but enough to say that this is by far one of my favorite games this year!

Long story short: Dude, Where's My Car 2: Desert Wasteland

First, let's talk about the Mad Max movies, which this game is obviously based on. Released in 1979, Mad Max was successful enough to spawn 2 more sequels, "The Road Warrior" and "Beyond Thunderdome". 30 years after Thunderdome, we were graced with a 4th Mad Max movie which most of you might know as "Fury Road". While the first Mad Max explored the origins of Max, its sequels retained the same theme. The story is set in a post-apocalyptic world where all the water of the world evaporated and global wars erupted. People kill and/or abuse each other in a savage tribal-like mentality. Max used to be a road patrol officer when he lost both his wife and daughter to a biker gang. Since then, he went rogue and is wandering the wasteland, helping those who need it and killing those standing in his way.

Now, let's ride on to the game itself.

Mad Max is an open world 3rd person beat-em-up game mixed with vehicular combat. You explore a large desert wasteland, destroying enemy camps to help friendly factions and loot their stuff to empower yourself. By completing in-game challenges and spending your Scrap (ingame money), you can unlock new weapons and equipment for both Max and his car. Melee combat feels very similar to the Batman serie; you punch enemies, parry their attacks and do follow-ups in a multi-directional free-form style allowing versatile and fluid combat. Vehicle combat is spiced up nicely with many ways to take down enemy cars and breaching camps.

On the art side, each character's costumes are well made. Of course, a desert wasteland isn't all that impressive or difficult to make, and this is why all the efforts went into the characters, cars and camps. Everything is made of rags, rusty pipes and generic garbage. It stays true to the movies' aesthetics.

In the sound department, the biggest star is Max's companion, Chumbucket, simply because he's the one who's got the most lines. Max does indeed speak, but he's not like the Mel-Gibson-Max, more like Tom-Hardy-Max, the one who doesn't talk all that much. Together, both create a great synergy. Max is a silent demented homicidal driver madman looking for his car and Chumbucket is his crazy-crazy car mechanic who has mental orgasms at the idea of upgrading Max's engine in the name of the "Angel Combustion".

After playing for a good half hour, it's clear this game is trying to carry on the soul of the Fury Road movie. It's jam-packed with action and car chases. It's wild and tribal. It also retains the same level of grit, going as far as being more gross and disgusting in some parts, due to implied cannibalism. This game also offer greater insight into Max's psyche. His encounter with Griffa, the "upgrade merchant", have been the most interesting story-wise for Max himself. Max is the kind of guy who could lose all his stuff but still find the strenght to survive, yet he's tormented, barely able to hang on in his absurd reality. In the end, I'm not sure if Griffa is even real at all and just an hallucination by Max.

Now, I'll talk about some of the regretable aspects of Mad Max.

First thing that comes to mind is the difficulty. There is no difficulty slider and it seems the game was made to be easy to appeal to casual gamer, mainly, people who watched Fury Road without ever playing a video game in their lives. Without any skills upgrade or armor, Max is like a demi-god. With added skills upgrade and armor, Max is god. Obviously, the game does get progressively harder as you get closer to the end, but most average gamers won't feel any pressure. Sure, you can ignore upgrades to "boost" difficulty but these upgrade are  fun to use in combat. Also, what doesn't help is the way the upgrade tree is made; almost everything can be unlocked right away, save for a few upgrades locked behind quests.

Secondly, I know this is supposed to be a desert wasteland full of nothing, but it felt like some content might have been missing. Evidence for this stems from certain ingame challenges that felt impossible to complete, like destroying 100 cars for both Scrotus and Roadkill faction. I spent 70 hours doing just that but these challenges appeared long after the final mission... A missing car combat arena of some sort, perhaps?

Speaking of upgrades, missing content and arenas... Why was there not a melee battle arena where completing challenges would earn you upgrades for Max instead of having them all unlocked right away? I guess I understand what "Beyond Thunderdome" means now... hehe...

Then there's Scrap, the in-game money. You use it for both Max's skill and his car upgrades. Why couldn't there be more specific pickup names, dividing the item types between Max and his car? What I'm saying is, instead of picking up Mufflers, Tires, Leather Pads and Gloves, there is only and only Scrap. Want to upgrade this or that? Just pick up that Scrap and stop thinking.

In the end, Mad Max is a game with amazing potential ultimately crushed by it's own ambitious scope. My inner child is saying "why cound't we have this or that", but my inner adult is saying "time and budget constraints". This is a video game adaptation of a movie after all. Like many, many other movie video games, time and budget is limited, and not all ideas put on the table can be executed. If the devs would've had more time to iron it out, Mad Max could have been an even more enjoyable experience, because it already is quite enjoyable nonetheless.

Last little technical note. It's not mandatory but it's preferable to use a controller to play this game. Combat and car controls just feels more smooth with it.

I recommend this game for fans of Mad Max and post-apocalyptic worlds. I rate this game a solid 7/10, loose 8/10.

While this game is slightly getting on now, having come out in 2015 and me first buying it in late 2017, it still stands up to games being released currently in terms of graphics and effects. The game is of couse set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, which gives it a ton of breathing room for showcasing the artistic talent of the art designers, which it does impressively - I often find myself on top of a rock staring out at the vast wasteland, looking forward to the next adventure in the stunning landscape that is the Great White and beyond.

Being an older game as I said, this means that it still runs impressively on hardware that wouldn't be considered top end these days - of couse you should check the recommended hardware requirements, but it runs on my £700 (Dec. 2017) PC at 60fps with little to no stutters, even as I travel at high speed through this large open world.

This is one of the most underrated games in the past few years.  The driving mechanics are fun, the upgrades are fun from each hub you unlock.  The playstyle melee vs ranged combat is well done to match the atmosphere of Max's world.

If you like Arkham City you probably will like this.  There is more vehicle combat (sadly like Arkham Knight) but in this game it is actually fun and the upgrades change what you can do.  

I should have written this review earlier.  I played it on Playstation 4 first and went through it twice then another 35 hours here.  Too bad it didn't catch on and we probably will never see a sequel.  This had a lot of potential if the developers would just add to the formula, not change it in the sequel unlike so many developers.

If you want a fun 20 hour campaign, 25 to 30 if you want to Max our the Car and Max's stats and a fun open world with a good mix of gameplay mechanics and story then look no further.

Sometimes you find a game that is 75% greatness and 25% copypasta. Mad Max the game is a great example of this. Driving around the wasteland feels incredibly exotic and atmospheric. Close combat is utterly bone-crunching and gives an original twist of the Batman Arkham classic system. I enjoyed particularly the use of limited, powerful resources... which are shivs and shotgun shells in fact, which is certainly true to the source material. Also the presentation is fantastic and tinkering your car, the Magnum Opus, is tremendous fun. Now that is a very solid 75% there and certainly worth the purchase and your 25-40 hours, if you are an open world fan or just love Mad Max, as we all should. Australian wastelands are always in fashion.

Now we get to the 25%, sadly. The crux of the gameplay and your objective basically, is to gather resources. You need a tremendous amount of that, which of course means grinding. Also, the storytelling is very bare bones and repetitive even. There is also tragic repetition in area boss fights, where you simply fight the same boss in different skins! You also need to accomplish map activities, which mainly include driving around to find them and doing the same things over and over. 

So my final verdict is to get it, but beforehand gauging your personal interest in open worlds at this point. Its very cheap on sale, which certainly makes it easier to recommend. If there ever was a game that needed more time in the oven, or better yet, a more refined sequel, it is Mad Max. On the other hand... if you are hungry for the kinds of things described, then this is certainly a delicious can of Dinki-Di dog food indeed.
